10.9. Validated Solvers and Certificate Workflows🔗

10.9.1. Validated Nonlinear Algebra🔗

Validated numerical work often begins with data that is useful but not yet a proof: an affine approximation, a narrow interval around a suspected root, or a floating-point approximation to a matrix inverse. Each kernel comes with the small mathematical obligation that turns such a proposal into an ordinary Lean theorem: an enclosure, a uniqueness claim, or an invertibility theorem.

An affine model, in FloatLib's affine arithmetic FloatLib.Numerics.Enclosure.Affine, consists of an exact rational affine form A(\varepsilon) and a rational interval R for the terms not retained in that form. It represents a real value x when

x-A(\varepsilon)\in R.

The reported range is the interval sum of the affine range and R. The noise variables are shared between occurrences of the same input coordinate, so the model retains dependencies that ordinary interval substitution would forget.

Suppose affine models M_A and M_B represent x and y at a common noise assignment satisfying |\varepsilon_i|\leq1. The checked product model represents xy at the same assignment.

Its affine part retains the constant and linear terms. Its interval remainder contains the quadratic noise product, the two affine-remainder cross terms, and the product of the old remainders.

Proof for Theorem 10.125
uses 0

Write x=A+r and y=B+s. Expand xy=AB+As+Br+rs, separate the constant-linear part of AB, and enclose the discarded quadratic term using \varepsilon_i^2\in[0,1] on the diagonal and \varepsilon_i\varepsilon_j\in[-1,1] off the diagonal. FloatLib's exact interval addition and multiplication theorems enclose the remaining three terms.

FloatLib's affine compiler Expr.affineModel? accepts rational constants, variables, addition, subtraction, negation, multiplication, and natural powers. A CAS expression reaches it through the translation into FloatLib's expression language, with one number for each variable. If the compiler returns a model for an expression on a rational box, every point of that box evaluates inside the model's reported range.

Each input interval is recentered as c_i+r_i\varepsilon_i. For any boxed point, the recovered noise lies in [-1,1] and recenters to the original point. On unsupported expression constructors the compiler fails.

Proof for Theorem 10.126
uses 0

Induct on the translated expression, using the affine semantic theorem for each accepted constructor. Recover one unit noise per input coordinate from the boxed point, prove its magnitude is at most one, and rewrite the recentered coordinates back to the original point. The model-range theorem then supplies the ordinary enclosure, and the translation's real-denotation equality returns it to the CAS expression.

A checked interval-Newton step for a rational univariate polynomial uses a nondegenerate input interval and a sign-definite interval enclosure of the derivative. It checks the proposed image against the exact Newton image computed from the midpoint. Every input root lies in that image.

For the checked Newton image N(I), the localization contract is

x\in I\ \land\ p(x)=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x\in N(I).

If endpoint signs bracket a root, derivative nonvanishing gives exactly one root in the input interval. If the checked image is disjoint from the input, the input interval contains no root:

N(I)\cap I=\varnothing \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \forall x\in I,\ p(x)\ne0.

Both conclusions are local to the stated interval.

Proof for Theorem 10.127
uses 0

The mean value theorem expresses a root relative to the interval midpoint. The derivative enclosure and its sign select a valid reciprocal interval, so interval arithmetic places the root in the proposed Newton image. Endpoint signs give existence by the intermediate value theorem and strict monotonicity gives uniqueness. Disjointness contradicts image membership and therefore proves root exclusion.

For p(x)=x^2-2 on I=[1,2], take the midpoint m=3/2. Then p(m)=1/4 and p'(I)\subseteq[2,4]. Any root z\in I satisfies 0=p(m)+p'(\xi)(z-m) for some intermediate \xi, hence

z\in m-\frac{p(m)}{[2,4]} =\frac32-\left[\frac1{16},\frac18\right] =\left[\frac{11}{8},\frac{23}{16}\right].

This narrows a width-one bracket to width 1/16. The endpoint signs p(1)<0<p(2) establish existence, and p'>0 establishes uniqueness. The Newton-image calculation localizes that root; its localization implication alone would also be true if there were no root.

For finite square matrices, an approximate-inverse candidate stores a target matrix A, a proposed inverse B, and a nonnegative residual bound \eta. The proposal contains no proof. Certification requires

\lVert I-BA\rVert\leq\eta<1

in Mathlib's Euclidean matrix operator norm.

Every certified approximate inverse proves that A is a unit and that its Euclidean continuous linear operator is bijective. It also gives the a posteriori estimate

\lVert A^{-1}-B\rVert \leq \eta\,\lVert A^{-1}\rVert.

The proposed inverse need not equal A^{-1}.

Proof for Theorem 10.129
uses 0

The strict residual bound makes I-(I-BA)=BA a unit by Mathlib's Neumann theorem. Direct finiteness of the square matrix algebra then implies that both factors B and A are units. Mapping the matrix unit into continuous linear maps gives bijectivity. Finally, A^{-1}-B=(I-BA)A^{-1} and norm submultiplicativity give the error bound.

An alternative checker accepts exact rational upper bounds u_{ij} for the absolute values of the entries of I-BA. If every row sum of these bounds is at most \eta<1, then the matrix infinity norm of the residual is below one and A is invertible.

This route matches the output of entrywise interval evaluation. Its conclusion is algebraic invertibility, so later Euclidean arguments do not need to identify the infinity norm with the Euclidean operator norm.

Let A(x) and the proposed inverse B(x) be square matrices of reflected real expressions. A constant rational matrix is one possible choice of B. The compiler forms I-B(x)A(x), evaluates every entry through one checked interval context, replaces each interval by its exact endpoint absolute maximum, and computes the largest rational row sum q.

If every entry compiles and q<1, then for every parameter point x in the context domain the real matrix A(x) is invertible. Failure of any entry or of the strict comparison returns none.

uses 0

Expression evaluation commutes with matrix multiplication, so the generated symbolic matrix denotes the actual residual I-B(x)A(x). Interval soundness bounds each residual entry. Summing endpoint absolute maxima bounds every row, and taking the finite maximum gives the advertised q. The checked row-sum Neumann theorem then proves invertibility pointwise.

used by 1✓L∃∀N

For a real map F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n, a ball-form Krawczyk proposal stores a center x_0, nonnegative radius r, real approximate-inverse matrix B, and nonnegative contraction bound q. Certification requires an actual Fréchet Jacobian J(x) on the closed ball together with

\lVert I-BJ(x)\rVert_2\leq q<1, \qquad \lVert BF(x_0)\rVert_2+qr\leq r.

For a fixed rational matrix B, the interval layer encloses the entries of J(x) and compiles those bounds to I-BJ(x). Its Frobenius checker computes the sum of squared endpoint absolute bounds in exact nonnegative-rational arithmetic. The certificate is stated for a closed Euclidean ball rather than for the rectangular boxes of the classical Krawczyk operator.

    def CAS.Continuum.Krawczyk.certifyFrobenius.{u_1} {n : Type u_1} [Fintype n]
  (bounds : Matrix n n CAS.Continuum.RationalInterval) (bound : ℚ≥0) :
  Bool
    def CAS.Continuum.Krawczyk.certifyFrobenius.{u_1}
  {n : Type u_1} [Fintype n]
  (bounds :
    Matrix n n
      CAS.Continuum.RationalInterval)
  (bound : ℚ≥0) : Bool

    Check a Frobenius proposal using exact nonnegative-rational arithmetic.

    Returning true means only that the executable rational comparison succeeded; certifyFrobenius_sound supplies its kernel-checked semantic interpretation.

The two inequalities have different jobs. For T(x)=x-BF(x), the Jacobian bound contracts distances throughout the ball. Writing \eta=\|BF(x_0)\|, the center moves by \eta, so

\|T(x)-x_0\| \leq\|T(x)-T(x_0)\|+\|T(x_0)-x_0\| \leq qr+\eta.

Thus \eta+qr\leq r keeps the entire image inside the ball. Equivalently, the radius must absorb the amplified center defect \eta/(1-q). This is the local finite-dimensional version of the defect estimate in the fixed-point chapter, with the self-map condition checked explicitly.

Proof for Theorem 10.133
uses 0

The map T(x)=x-BF(x) has derivative I-BJ(x), hence is q-Lipschitz on the convex ball. The self-map inequality sends that ball into itself, so Banach's fixed-point theorem gives a unique fixed point. At the center, the same strict residual estimate proves BJ(x_0) and then B invertible by the Neumann argument. Thus T(x)=x implies BF(x)=0 and hence F(x)=0. Conversely every zero is a fixed point, which transfers fixed-point uniqueness to zero uniqueness.

10.9.2. Certificate Workflows🔗

Checked numerical certificates enter an ordinary Lean proof through the cega tactic, which can project a supplied certificate or construct one through a checked rational-box query. For an ordinary inequality goal, bare cega can read the box off rational literal bounds among the hypotheses; explicit box syntax supplies the query directly. In either route, a checked soundness proof must establish the target, including any domain or error weakening.

An independently certified numerical value may replace the exact-real quadrature value. Its roundoff bound is added to the analytic quadrature error by the triangle inequality. The theorem is the common interface for a verified exact, interval, or floating-point implementation: a backend must prove the displayed norm bound before its computed value enters the quadrature certificate.

Concretely, if Q is the value stored in a certificate with error E and \widehat Q is a computed replacement satisfying \lVert Q-\widehat Q\rVert\leq\delta, then

\left\lVert\int_a^b f(x)\,dx-\widehat Q\right\rVert \leq E+\delta.

Approximation, residual, upper-bound, enclosure, and model-approximation certificates may be restricted from a domain s to any subset t ⊆ s. The resulting theorem is the original sound field composed with the subset proof; no backend computation is repeated.

For every semantic predicate P, the restriction step is simply

t\subseteq s,\qquad \bigl(\forall x\in s,\ P(x)\bigr) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \forall x\in t,\ P(x).

The certificate-projection route of cega searches the local context and target for a recognized checked certificate. It first tries the certificate's semantic theorem exactly, then permits a proved domain restriction, a larger error budget, or a wider enclosure when those changes match the goal. Any new real inequalities are discharged separately by ordinary arithmetic. The tactic succeeds only after Lean confirms that the constructed proof has the user's target type.

For an approximation certificate, the representative projection is

t\subseteq s,\quad c.\mathrm{eps}\leq\varepsilon \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \forall x\in t,\qquad \lVert c.\mathrm{lhs}(x)-c.\mathrm{rhs}(x)\rVert\leq\varepsilon.

Residual, bound, enclosure, model, and quadrature goals use the analogous typed projection; cega never changes the proposition being proved.

    def CAS.Tactic.Certificate.closeFromLocalCertificates :
  Lean.Elab.Tactic.TacticM Unit

    Close the main goal from a matching checked certificate in the local context or among the subterms of the target.

    Exact projections are tried first. Approximation, residual, bound, model, and quadrature certificates may then be weakened to a larger requested budget; enclosures may be widened at both endpoints. Every generated inequality must be discharged by the shared arithmetic phase. A certificate whose domain differs from the goal's is then restricted to the goal's domain (inferSubsetProof) and tried again in the same way.

Certificate example: cosine near the origin.

PDE/Examples/Numerics/CosineEnclosure.lean compiles a complete enclosure of Real.cos on

D=\left[-\frac1{10},\frac1{10}\right].

CEGA certifies [199/200,1] on D. The interval and its proof are stored as CAS.Examples.Numerics.CosineEnclosure.cosineEnclosure, an EnclosureCert ℝ D whose fields have the following meaning:

  • fn is Real.cos;

  • lo is 199 / 200;

  • hi is 1;

  • sound proves 199/200\leq\cos x\leq1 for every x\in D.

The theorem-facing use is short:

-- Import the backend-independent certificate propositions. open CAS.Certificate -- CEGA projects the certificate's soundness -- theorem into the target. example (domain : Set ℝ) (cosineEnclosure : EnclosureCert ℝ domain) : EnclosedOn cosineEnclosure.fn domain cosineEnclosure.lo cosineEnclosure.hi := domain:Set ℝcosineEnclosure:EnclosureCert ℝ domain⊢ EnclosedOn cosineEnclosure.fn domain cosineEnclosure.lo cosineEnclosure.hi All goals completed! 🐙

The tactic projects the stored theorem; cosine is not evaluated again.

The same object can support a smaller domain. Given D'\subseteq D, cosineEnclosure.restrict D' hsub stores the same function and endpoints with soundness restricted along hsub. It can also support a coarser conclusion: EnclosureCert.weaken turns [199/200,1] into any proved wider interval, for example [-1,1]. These operations are set inclusion and transitivity proofs.

The generic proof pattern is therefore:

-- A certificate on s proves the same -- enclosure on a subset t. example {s t : Set ℝ} (c : EnclosureCert ℝ s) (hsub : t ⊆ s) : EnclosedOn c.fn t c.lo c.hi := s:Set ℝt:Set ℝc:EnclosureCert ℝ shsub:t ⊆ s⊢ EnclosedOn c.fn t c.lo c.hi All goals completed! 🐙

Here cega finds the domain restriction needed to match the target.

An ODETrajectoryCert stores an ordinary Lean curve, its proposed velocity, continuity on [a,b], a proof that the velocity is its right derivative on [a,b), membership in the state region, and one backend-independent residual bound for u'(t)-F(t,u(t)). Mathlib's approximate-trajectory Grönwall theorem compares two such trajectories. The pointwise estimate is converted to a uniform ApproxCert by evaluating the monotone Grönwall bound at the right endpoint. No ordering hypothesis is needed: if the left endpoint is below the right one, residual soundness there makes both budgets nonnegative, and otherwise the claim is immediate.

As an example, the affine Euler curve 1+t is compared with the exact trajectory \exp t for u'=u on [0,1]. Its residual is -t, hence has norm at most one, and the generated uniform error is \exp(1)-1. An exact CAS proof or a FloatLib enclosure may supply the residual bound. The ODE stability theorem consumes that real bound and gives the same final ApproxOn statement.

Proof for Theorem 10.137
uses 0

The residual certificate bounds the defect between the proposed velocity and the vector field. Apply the approximate-trajectory Grönwall estimate to this defect and the initial discrepancy, then use monotonicity of the exponential bound to replace its time-dependent right-hand side by its value at the final time. This produces the uniform approximation certificate.

The stability estimate explains how the residual enters the trajectory error. If the vector field is L-Lipschitz in the state variable, the initial discrepancy is e_0, and the sum of the two residual budgets is \delta, Grönwall gives, for L>0,

\|u(t)-v(t)\| \leq e^{L(t-a)}e_0+ \delta\,\frac{e^{L(t-a)}-1}{L}.

For L=0, the corresponding bound is e_0+\delta(t-a). In the 1+t versus e^t example, e_0=0, L=1, and \delta=1, giving the stated e-1 budget at time one. The actual maximum error is e-2: the certificate is conservative because it replaces the varying defect t by the uniform bound one. Both curves are hypotheses of the comparison theorem.

Under the trapezoidal regularity and second-derivative-bound hypotheses, one user-supplied tolerance can control analytic truncation and verified numerical error. Let I have radius r<\mathrm{tolerance}. The enclosure proof must refer to the exact-real trapezoidal value on the mesh planned with the budget \mathrm{tolerance}-r. Replacing that exact rule value by the interval midpoint then has total certified error at most the original tolerance.

Patch covers assemble local approximation or residual proofs into a global theorem on the covered domain. The atlas layer, used near singularities or across piecewise regimes, rests on this theorem.

The shared logical contract is

\left(\forall x\in s,\ \exists i,\ x\in s_i\right) \land \left(\forall i,\ \forall x\in s_i,\ P(x)\right) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \forall x\in s,\ P(x).

For approximation and residual atlases, P(x) is the corresponding stored norm bound.

Fix a point in the global domain and use the cover property to choose a patch containing it. The local certificate on that patch proves the desired predicate at the point. Since the argument is independent of the selected patch, it assembles the local soundness fields into the global theorem.

External data and analytic proofs.

A numerical solver can propose rational coefficients, interval endpoints, or binary64 words in JSON. The exact-data importer embeds integer columns as Lean data, rejecting incorrect lengths and invalid word ranges. Decimal strings preserve large integers even when the producer's JSON tools use floating point. The data file is a Lake dependency, so changing it invalidates the build trace. Importing those values proves no numerical or analytic property.

Proof for Theorem 10.140
uses 0

For index i and batch size b>0, Euclidean division writes i=b\lfloor i/b\rfloor+(i\bmod b). The remainder lies in its batch, including the shorter final batch. Apply that batch's check and then the analytic soundness theorem. The empty domain needs no checks.

The tactic forms cega [batch := 128] and cega [fast, batch := 128] generate these internal proof steps without numbered source modules. The fast form follows the configured native/kernel checking profile. Native checking additionally trusts Lean's compiler and runtime; kernel checking computes the same proposition and can take longer.

The analytic bridge remains essential. Bounds at sampled points alone do not control the function between them: an interval cover, interpolation estimate, derivative remainder, or stability theorem must supply that argument. In the De Gregorio spline construction, verified smoothing replay identifies the candidate values, exact row checks bound the linear-system residual, and diagonal dominance converts that budget to an error bound against the exact slope vector.

The public query layer accepts an arbitrary finite rational box and reports failure unless it can produce a proof. One successful enclosure supplies four theorems: the two-sided range, an ordinary upper bound, a bound for the magnitude, and uniform approximation by the rational center with the rational radius as error. Each theorem connects the executable query result to an ordinary semantic proposition. Route steps remain diagnostic metadata.

Writing B=\prod_i[a_i,b_i] and [\ell,h] for the certified interval of a successful enclosure of e on B, the four contracts are

\begin{aligned} &\forall x\in B,\quad \ell\leq e(x)\leq h,\\ &\forall x\in B,\quad e(x)\leq h,\\ &\forall x\in B,\quad |e(x)|\leq\max(|\ell|,|h|),\\ &\forall x\in B,\quad \left|e(x)-\tfrac{\ell+h}{2}\right|\leq\tfrac{h-\ell}{2}. \end{aligned}

  CAS.Certificate.ApproxOn fn
    (fun x ↦ ↑center) s ↑radius

    Restate the midpoint approximation using displayed rational data.

Proof for Theorem 10.141
uses 0

Successful interval evaluation first supplies a two-sided enclosure for every point of the input box. The enclosure query returns it directly; the upper-bound and absolute-bound queries project elementary consequences of its endpoints; and the midpoint query rewrites membership in the interval as a distance bound from its center. Each projection preserves the evaluator's quantification over the whole domain.

How the certificate layer fits together.

Exact symbolic proofs are the zero-error case. Approximation certificates add a uniform error, enclosure certificates retain a function and scalar endpoints, and quadrature certificates combine an exact-real rule with an analytic remainder. Patch covers glue pointwise identities, enclosures, and uniform error bounds on a covered domain. Quadrature certificates on adjacent oriented intervals compose using interval integrability and integral additivity, with their error budgets added.

For PDE applications, the patch theorem's pointwise conclusion should be kept explicit. A piecewise constant function can have classical derivative zero on both sides of an interface while its distributional derivative contains a jump term at that interface. Covering those open pieces and checking their residuals does not settle the interface equation. A weak solution assembled from local pieces also needs the appropriate matching or flux conditions, as well as integrability.
